name: Cryogenics Must Scale
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Refrigerator Problem: Why You Cannot Just Build a Bigger Fridge
lesson.summary: Today's qubits need cooling to a fraction of a degree above absolute zero, and the wiring required to control each one competes directly with the cooling power available to keep them cold, a bottleneck that does not disappear by scaling up existing fridges.
lesson.body:
Superconducting qubits, the kind used by most major quantum computing efforts, only behave like qubits at extraordinarily low temperatures, typically around ten to fifteen millikelvin, a small fraction of a degree above absolute zero. At any warmer temperature, thermal noise from the surrounding environment overwhelms the delicate quantum states the computer depends on. Getting there requires a dilution refrigerator: a room-sized, enormously expensive piece of equipment that takes hours to cool down and offers only a limited amount of cooling power at its coldest stage.

Here is the part that rarely makes it into the headlines. Every single qubit needs its own physical control and readout wiring, typically coaxial cables, running from room-temperature electronics all the way down through the fridge's cooling stages to the chip itself. Those wires are not free: each one is a physical channel that carries a small amount of heat down into the coldest part of the fridge, working directly against the cooling the fridge is trying to provide. A chip with a hundred qubits might already need hundreds of individual cables threading through a cramped, multi-stage cryostat. Scaling up a thousandfold, toward the qubit counts many algorithms would actually need, means either the wiring problem gets solved through a completely different approach, or it does not scale at all.

The proposed fix is called cryo-CMOS: specialized control chips placed inside the fridge itself, close to the qubits, so that only a handful of wires need to run all the way down from room temperature, with the fridge-local chip handling the multiplexing and control logic for many qubits at once. This sounds straightforward until you remember that ordinary electronics were never designed to operate reliably at fifteen millikelvin, and that the cryo-CMOS chips themselves generate heat that has to be managed inside an already heat-constrained environment. It is a genuinely unsolved engineering problem, not a matter of simply commissioning a larger dilution fridge from a supplier.

It is worth noting that not every qubit technology needs quite this extreme an environment. Trapped-ion and some photonic approaches can operate at less severe temperatures. But every architecture still faces some version of the same underlying tension: more qubits mean more control channels, and more control channels mean more competition for whatever cooling or isolation budget the system has. Cryogenics is on the list of required breakthroughs precisely because it is a hard physical constraint that exists independently of how good the qubits themselves eventually become.
